title: 05 · d · p · q · r
summary: Four functions per distribution; the first letter is the question: exactly (d), at most (p), which value (q), random values (r).
question: How do you ask R a probability question about a distribution?

chain.title: Prefix + name = function
chain.statement: Each distribution has four functions; the prefix d, p, q or r is the question, the name (binom, pois, norm, unif) the distribution.

explain.text: binom counts successes in n trials (arguments size, prob; mean np); pois counts with no upper limit (lambda; variance = mean); norm describes measurements (mean, sd; the bell curve); unif gives equal chances between min and max. So dbinom, pbinom, qbinom and rbinom ask the four questions of the binomial, and the same pattern holds for the other three.
The running example (Lecture 4): about 7% of lymphocytes are natural killer (NK) cells. Take 10 cells; the number of NK cells among them is binomial with size = 10 and prob = 0.07.

terms.meaning: successes in size independent trials, each with probability prob
counts of events with mean lambda, no upper limit; variance = mean
bell-shaped distribution of measurements with mean and sd
every value between min and max equally likely

chain.intuition: The prefix is the question word, the name is the subject.
chain.misconception: qnorm and pnorm do the same thing. They are inverses: p takes a value and gives a probability; q takes a probability and gives a value.

check.q: Which function simulates 100 Poisson counts with mean 3?

chain.opens: How likely is exactly 2 NK cells among 10?
chain.answers: How do you ask R a probability question about a distribution?

chain.title: d: how likely is exactly this value?
chain.statement: dbinom(2, size = 10, prob = 0.07) = 0.1233878 is the probability of exactly 2 NK cells among 10.

explain.text: The binomial formula counts the ways to choose which 2 of the 10 cells are NK (45 ways) and multiplies by the chance of that pattern: 0.07² for the two NK cells and 0.93⁸ for the eight others. About one sample of ten in eight holds exactly two NK cells.

figure.caption: P(X = 2) is one bar of the binomial with size 10, prob 0.07.

examples.title: Exactly 2 NK cells
examples.problem: 7% of lymphocytes are NK cells; in 10 cells, what is P(exactly 2)?

solution.text: Ways to choose the two NK cells:

lines.explain: d = P(exactly x); x = 2 successes, size = 10 trials, prob = 0.07 per trial

code.interpret: About a 12% chance of exactly two NK cells in ten.

terms.meaning: the number of ways to choose x items from size

chain.intuition: d picks one bar of the distribution.
chain.misconception: For continuous data, dnorm() is also P(exactly x). It is the curve's height; any exact value has probability 0.

right.title: Instead
right.text: dbinom gives a probability; dnorm gives a height.

check.q: What is P(no NK cell in 10)?

chain.opens: How likely is this value or fewer?
chain.answers: How likely is exactly 2 NK cells among 10?

chain.title: p: this value or less
chain.statement: pbinom(3, size = 10, prob = 0.07) = 0.9964239 adds the bars for 0, 1, 2 and 3: the probability of no more than 3 NK cells.

explain.text: p means cumulative: P(X ≤ x). Here 0.484 + 0.364 + 0.123 + 0.025 = 0.996. "More than 3" is the complement, so flip it: 1 − pbinom(3, …) = 0.0036, about 4 samples in 1,000.

figure.caption: P(X ≤ 3): the bars 0 to 3 added up.

examples.title: At most 3, and more than 3
examples.problem: P(X ≤ 3) and P(X > 3) for 10 cells with prob 0.07.

lines.explain: p = P(X ≤ 3): sums the probabilities of 0, 1, 2 and 3

code.interpret: Four or more NK cells in ten would be rare (0.4%).

terms.meaning: P(X ≤ x): the sum (or area) up to x

chain.intuition: p is a running total from the left.
chain.misconception: 1 − pbinom(3) is P(X ≥ 3). It is P(X > 3); P(X ≥ 3) is 1 − pbinom(2).

misconceptionFigure.caption: X > 3 starts at 4; X ≥ 3 starts at 3.

chain.opens: Which value cuts off a given probability?
chain.answers: How likely is this value or fewer?

chain.title: q: which value cuts off this much?
chain.statement: qnorm(0.975) = 1.959964: 97.5% of a standard normal lies below 1.96. q reverses p: pnorm(1.96) ≈ 0.975.

explain.text: q takes a probability and returns the value that cuts it off on the left. For the standard normal (mean 0, sd 1), 2.5% lies above 1.96 and, by symmetry, 2.5% below −1.96, so 95% lies between them. That is the 1.96 in a 95% confidence interval: mean ± 1.96 standard errors (Bradley §3).

figure.caption: 97.5% of the standard normal lies left of 1.96.

lines.explain: q = the value with 97.5% of the standard normal below it
p = the area left of 1.96; the inverse question

examples.title: 95% interval for the mean sleep (added)
examples.problem: Mean sleep 10.53 h, SE 0.605 h (sheet 01). Give an approximate 95% interval.

source.title: Statistics notes: Standard deviations and standard errors
source.authors: Altman D G; Bland J M

terms.meaning: the value below which a given proportion of the distribution lies

chain.intuition: p goes from a value to an area; q goes from an area back to the value.
chain.misconception: qnorm(0.95) gives the 95% interval limit. That is 1.645, a one-sided cut; the two-sided 95% limit is qnorm(0.975).

check.q: What does qnorm(0.5) return, and why?
check.a: 0: half of a symmetric distribution centred at 0 lies below 0.

chain.opens: How do you make R generate random values from a distribution?
chain.answers: Which value cuts off a given probability?

chain.title: r: random values
chain.statement: rbinom(n = 10, size = 1, prob = 0.5) simulates 10 fair coin flips, e.g. 0 0 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 0: 6 heads, so the estimate is p ≈ 0.6.

explain.text: n is how many draws, size the trials per draw (1 = one coin flip, a 0 or a 1). Each run gives new values; set.seed(1) fixes the random generator so the same values come back. With more flips the share of heads closes in on 0.5: random variation shrinks as the sample grows.

figure.caption: Heads in 10 flips: random draws pile up into the binomial bars.

lines.explain: fix the random generator so the run can be repeated
10 draws, each one flip of a fair coin (1 = heads)
share of heads in 1000 flips: close to 0.5

code.interpret: 6 heads in 10 is an ordinary result for a fair coin; 1000 flips pin p down far better.

terms.meaning: fix the start of the random generator so results repeat
learning about a distribution by drawing from it many times

chain.intuition: r is the coin; d, p and q are the maths about the coin.

intuitionFigure.caption: The ten flips of the sheet: 6 heads, 4 tails.

chain.misconception: Getting 6 heads in 10 means the coin is biased. P(6 or more of 10) for a fair coin is 0.377: very common.

right.title: Instead
right.text: 6/10 happens 38% of the time with a fair coin.

check.q: Why does set.seed(1) matter in a report?
check.a: Readers can rerun the code and get the same random values, so the results are reproducible.

demos.title: Coin-flip machine
demos.purpose: How do random 0/1 draws add up to a stable share of heads?
demos.request: A coin-flipping machine that drops coins into two tubes (heads/tails) with a running share-of-heads readout; parameter n flips and prob; lessons show 10 flips (6 heads), 100, 1000 approaching 0.5.

chain.opens: Why do "less than" and "at most" give different answers for counts?
chain.answers: How do you make R generate random values from a distribution?

chain.title: Discrete: "less than" ≠ "at most"
chain.statement: For counts, X ≤ 3 is pbinom(3, …), X < 3 is pbinom(2, …), X > 3 is 1 − pbinom(3, …) and X ≥ 3 is 1 − pbinom(2, …).

explain.text: A count can be exactly 3, so whether 3 is included changes the answer. pbinom(k) always includes k. "Fewer than 3" stops at 2; "3 or more" removes everything up to 2. Translate the words into ≤ or < first, then into the call.

code.interpret: Including or excluding 3 changes the answer by P(X = 3) = 0.025.

terms.meaning: takes separate values (0, 1, 2 …), each with its own probability

chain.intuition: On a staircase, "up to step 3" and "below step 3" are different heights.

intuitionFigure.caption: The difference is one bar: P(X = 3).

chain.misconception: P(X < 3) = pbinom(3). That includes 3; use pbinom(2).

check.q: How do you get P(X ≥ 1) quickly?

chain.opens: How do you ask about a continuous variable, where no single value has a probability?
chain.answers: Why do "less than" and "at most" give different answers for counts?

chain.title: Continuous: ask about ranges
chain.statement: Any exact value of a continuous variable has probability 0, so subtract areas: pnorm(170, 165.1, 7.07) − pnorm(165, 165.1, 7.07) = 0.26 of women are 165–170 cm tall (Lecture 6).

explain.text: Heights follow a normal curve with mean 165.1 cm and sd 7.07 cm. The probability of a range is the area under the curve between its ends: the area left of 170 minus the area left of 165, 0.756 − 0.494 = 0.26.

figure.caption: Women between 165 and 170 cm: the shaded area.

lines.explain: minus the area left of 165 cm

code.interpret: About a quarter of women are between 165 and 170 cm.

terms.meaning: takes any value in a range; probabilities are areas under the curve

chain.intuition: Probability is paint on the floor under the curve; a line has no area.
chain.misconception: dnorm(170, 165.1, 7.07) is the share of women exactly 170 cm. It is a height of the curve (0.044 per cm), not a probability.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Shares are areas: use pnorm() differences.

check.q: What share of women is taller than 180 cm?
